beats.text: An algorithm is a precise sequence of steps for solving a class of problems. To find ten in this sorted list, binary search compares with a middle value instead of inspecting every entry from the beginning.

beats.formula: 10>8 quad arrow.r quad "keep the right half"
beats.text: Comparing ten with the lower middle value eight eliminates every entry up to eight. Sorted order justifies the elimination: none of those smaller values can be the target. The remaining candidates are ten, twelve, fourteen, and sixteen.

Comparing with twelve narrows the search again, leaving ten as the only candidate on its left. Each step preserves the invariant that a present target remains inside the candidate range. Shrinking that range ensures the procedure eventually terminates.

Repeated halving explains the logarithmic growth in comparisons. This efficiency depends on ordered data and a method for accessing middle entries. Without sorted order, discarding half could throw away the target, so speed cannot replace the algorithm's assumptions.

practice.prompt: Use binary search to find 11 in [1,3,5,7,9,11,13]. State each middle comparison.
practice.answer: Compare with 7, then keep [9,11,13]. Its middle is 11, so the target is found after two comparisons.

practice.prompt: Why is ordinary binary search invalid on [9,1,7,3,5]? Use target 3 and the middle value 7 to explain the failure.
practice.answer: The list is unsorted. Comparing 3<7 would discard the right side, but the target 3 is on that discarded side. Sorted order is needed for the elimination rule.

practice.prompt: Starting with 1,024 candidates, how many remain after ten exact halvings? Does this by itself prove that an arbitrary search procedure is correct?
practice.answer: 1,024/2¹⁰=1 remains. No: correctness also needs an invariant ensuring the target was never discarded and a valid stopping rule, possibly including a final comparison.

takeaway: An algorithm needs justified steps, a correctness invariant, and termination; efficiency depends on its assumptions.
scope: Binary search as a concrete example of algorithm design, correctness, and logarithmic work.
title: Algorithms
objective: Specify procedures and justify correctness, termination, and complexity.
